headline: Argentina offers passports to wealthy foreigners

sources.title: Debt-saddled Argentina pitches 'golden passport' scheme to woo wealthy foreigners (AP)
Pay for passports: Milei government unveils citizen by investment scheme (Buenos Aires Times)
Argentina to sell citizenship to foreigners for US$350,000 to raise dollars (MercoPress)
Argentine Citizenship Will Be New 'Status Symbol' For Wealthy Americans, Say Experts (video, Forbes Breaking News)

chunks.text: On October 2, 2026, Argentina announced a plan to offer [[citizenship]] to wealthy foreigners. The country's economy minister {{laid out}} the plan at an investor event in Paris. Applicants could make a [[nonrefundable]] payment of 350,000 dollars to the national [[treasury]]. Or they could buy a new government [[bond]] worth 800,000 dollars and {{hold on to}} it for seven years. [[Applications]] are expected to open before the end of 2026.

verbs.correct: To explain a plan in detail
verbs.wrong: To vote against a new law
verbs.why: The coach laid out the game plan before the match. The mayor laid out her plan for three new parks. The economy minister laid out the citizenship plan at an event in Paris.

verbs.correct: To keep something instead of selling it
verbs.wrong: To pay a small fee every month
verbs.why: He held on to his house when prices fell. My grandmother held on to her gold coins for years. Bond buyers would have to hold on to the new bond for seven years.

chunks.text: The plan is meant to {{bring in}} [[foreign currency]]. Argentina's treasury must make nearly 25 billion dollars in foreign-currency [[debt payments]] in 2027. The government has {{held off}} on a return to international bond markets. So it is {{turning to}} other sources of money. Its advisers say the program could raise up to 2.5 billion dollars. Dollars matter to President Javier Milei, who plans to seek [[reelection]] in 2027.

verbs.why: The bake sale brought in 500 dollars for the school. Tourism brings in a lot of money for the city. The citizenship plan is meant to bring in foreign currency.

verbs.wrong: To change the value of money
verbs.why: We held off on buying a house until prices fell. She held off on telling her parents the news. The government has held off on a return to international bond markets.

verbs.correct: To seek help from another source
verbs.why: When I lost my job, I turned to my family. Many students turn to online videos for help with math. With fewer ways to borrow, the government is turning to other sources of money.

chunks.text: About 60 countries give [[residency]] to foreigners who invest. Only about a dozen sell full citizenship, including several small Caribbean islands. Argentina would be the first in South America. The minister said the idea {{came up}} during a 2024 visit by Milei to the United States, when tech [[executives]] showed interest. Experts say more Americans and Europeans want a second country to {{fall back on}}. The government hopes to {{cash in on}} that [[demand]].

verbs.wrong: To be sold at a low price
verbs.why: Your name came up at the meeting. The idea of a trip came up over dinner. The idea for the program came up during a 2024 visit by Milei to the United States.

verbs.correct: To use something if other plans fail
verbs.wrong: To leave your own home country
verbs.why: She has savings to fall back on if she loses her job. If the bus is late, I can fall back on my bike. More Americans and Europeans want a second country to fall back on.

verbs.correct: To use a chance to earn money
verbs.why: Hotels cash in on the big game every year. Toy stores cash in on the weeks before Christmas. The government hopes to cash in on the demand for a second passport.

chunks.text: Such programs have long faced [[criticism]]. A global [[watchdog]] has warned that criminals use them to hide [[illegal money]]. In April 2025, the European Union's top court ruled that Malta's program was [[unlawful]]. Other countries have {{shut down}} programs that sold residency. The minister said [[intelligence]] and financial agencies will check each applicant's [[criminal record]] and [[source of funds]]. The goal is to {{weed out}} criminals. All money must go through the official [[financial system]]. Immigration officials will approve or {{turn down}} each application.

verbs.correct: To close and stop a program
verbs.why: The city shut down the program after two years. The school shut down its night classes. Some countries have shut down programs that sold residency.

verbs.correct: To find and remove unwanted people
verbs.why: The first interview weeds out people who are not serious. Online tests help weed out weak job applicants. Checks on each applicant are meant to weed out criminals.

verbs.correct: To say no to a request
verbs.why: She turned down the job offer. The bank turned down his loan request. Immigration officials will approve or turn down each citizenship application.

mainIdea.s: Argentina wants to offer passports to rich foreigners who pay the state or buy a special bond. The government badly needs dollars, since huge debt payments are due in 2027.
mainIdea.why: The plan is meant to bring in foreign currency. The treasury must make nearly 25 billion dollars in debt payments in 2027.

mainIdea.s: Thousands of wealthy foreigners have already paid for Argentine citizenship this fall. Their money has now covered most of what the country owes to lenders next year.
mainIdea.why: Close, but applications are only expected to open before the end of 2026. Advisers think the program could bring in up to 2.5 billion dollars.

mainIdea.s: Argentina has passed a new law that makes it harder for its own citizens to travel abroad. They now need a special travel permit and must pay a new fee at the airport.
mainIdea.why: The economy minister laid out a plan to sell citizenship to wealthy foreigners. It is meant to raise dollars for the country.

tf.s: The economy minister laid out a plan to sell citizenship to rich foreigners.
tf.why: Argentina's economy minister laid out a plan to offer citizenship to wealthy foreigners who pay or invest.

tf.s: The plan is mainly meant to bring in tourists, not foreign currency.
tf.why: The plan is meant to bring in foreign currency, because Argentina has large debt payments to make.

tf.s: Argentina would be the first country in South America to sell citizenship.
tf.why: Only about a dozen countries sell citizenship, and Argentina hopes the plan will bring in foreign currency.

tf.s: Applicants will not face any checks on their criminal records.
tf.why: Intelligence and financial agencies will check each applicant, and the goal is to weed out criminals.

tf.s: Argentina has recently returned to international bond markets.
tf.why: The government has held off on a return to those markets, so it is turning to other sources of money.

tf.s: Immigration officials will approve or turn down each application.
tf.why: After the checks, immigration officials decide on every application, and they can turn down any applicant.

lines.text: Did you hear that Argentina wants to sell passports?
To wealthy foreigners. The economy minister {{laid out}} the plan in Paris.
You either give the government 350,000 dollars, or you buy an 800,000-dollar bond and {{hold on to}} it for seven years.
That's a lot. Why would anyone pay that much?
The passport lets you visit more than 140 countries without a visa first. For some rich people, it's a [[Plan B]].
So, a second country to {{fall back on}} if things get bad at home.
Right. It gives them [[peace of mind]].
Dollars. Advisers think it could {{bring in}} up to 2.5 billion. The country owes nearly 25 billion in 2027.
[[I can see why]] they want the money. But it [[makes you wonder]] who will apply.
That's the worry. Criminals have used programs like this to hide illegal money.
Will Argentina check the people who apply?
Officials say they'll {{weed out}} anyone with a criminal past and {{turn down}} any application that fails the checks.
Some countries have {{shut down}} programs like this, right?
Yes. It raises a big question. Should rich people be able to buy citizenship?
[[That's a tough one]]. I'd want to see how it works first.
